Subject: Wellsford Road: what we got wrong, and what we are changing

DRAFT — for standards review only. Not for publication or scheduling.

By Nell Garside

Our article of 2 November put Wellsford Road first in a table of Bristol roads ranked by recorded injury collisions, with 41 over the five years from 2021 to 2025. That figure was wrong. The correct total is 23, placing the road sixth.

The article and table have carried the correction since Friday, 6 November. But changing the number does not explain how we arrived at it, or answer the residents who had good reason to question it. With more than 48,000 page views on the original story, the wrong figure reached a substantial audience. We cannot assume that everyone who saw it has seen the correction.

A member of the Fishponds Streets Forum checked the published Department for Transport data herself and could not reproduce our total. She was right. The forum also told us that parents were asking whether it was safe to walk their children to Wellsford Primary. I am sorry for the concern our incorrect reporting caused residents and families, and for giving readers a figure they could not rely on.

What went wrong

The error occurred when we combined records to associate collisions with roads. That operation, known as a join, duplicated some collision–road pairs. In plain terms, the same collision appeared twice in a road’s tally, and our analysis counted both entries.

We removed 18 duplicate entries from Wellsford Road’s total, mostly at its junctions with Pell Street and Kingsmere Road. These were not additional collisions, nor were they collisions we subsequently decided to exclude. They were repeated entries for collisions already counted.

The corrected method counts each unique accident reference, called an accident index in the source data, once per road. We reran the whole citywide table, not just Wellsford Road’s figures.

The corrected top six are:

1. Kingsmere Road: 32 injury collisions
2. Alder Hill: 31
3. Tanner’s Way: 28
4. Crossfield Road: 26
5. Hambrook Lane: 24
6. Wellsford Road: 23

This was our error as a desk. Our checks should have caught the duplication before publication, and they did not.

What the corrected figures do—and do not—tell us

Of the 23 recorded injury collisions on Wellsford Road, three were serious and none was fatal. The description circulating locally of it as Bristol’s “deadliest road” is not supported by these figures.

That does not mean the road is fine. Twenty-three injury collisions remain 23 injury collisions, with consequences for the people involved. Correcting an inflated total is not a reason to dismiss residents’ concerns.

Nor can a ranking of raw collision totals answer a parent’s question about the safety of a particular walk to school. It does not account for how many people use each road or the conditions at individual crossings and junctions. Our table counts recorded injury collisions within the city council boundary; it is not a complete assessment of road safety.

What changes now

From now on, we will publish the cleaned dataset and analysis code alongside our ranked tables, so readers can see how the figures were produced. A second analyst will independently reproduce each ranked table before publication. That check must establish that the result can be obtained again, rather than simply that the finished table looks plausible.

I would also welcome the opportunity to attend the Fishponds Streets Forum meeting at Fishponds Library on 17 November, at 7pm, to explain the correction and answer questions in person.

Readers should not have to redo our analysis to discover an error of this kind. When they do challenge our work, they are owed a proper answer.
